title: Growers and Houses
subtitle: Who grows champagne's grapes, who makes and sells the wine, and how the two have needed each other for three centuries.

episodes.title: Two Sides of One Wine
episodes.hook: Behind almost every bottle of champagne stand two kinds of people: the families who farm the vines, and the houses who turn grapes into a wine with a famous name. This thread follows how they came to need each other.
cards: For most of its history, Champagne has been a region where the people who grew the grapes and the people who made the wine were usually not the same people.
On one side are the growers, the vignerons, who farm the vineyards village by village, often on small holdings passed down through many generations.
On the other side are the houses, the maisons, which buy grapes or young wine, make champagne in their cellars and sell it under their own names around the world.
The Comité Champagne, the joint body of growers and houses, counted 16,460 growers, 120 cooperatives and 410 houses in its figures for 2025.
Those counts move a little from year to year, and older sources give other totals, so it is always worth checking which year a number describes.
Between them, the growers farm close to nine-tenths of the vineyard area. The houses hold the rest, a little over a tenth, according to the houses' own trade union.
The area in production stood at about 34,200 hectares in the Comité's 2025 figures, so the houses' share of the land comes to only a few thousand hectares in all.
The bottles tell the opposite story. Of roughly 266 million bottles shipped in 2025, the houses shipped about 192 million, a little over seven in every ten.
Growers who make and sell their own champagne shipped about 51 million bottles, a little under one in five, and the cooperatives about 23 million, a little under one in ten.
Those last two figures come from a trade analysis of the Comité's data. Its total differs very slightly from the Comité's own, which leaves the proportions unchanged.
Measured by value rather than by bottles, the houses' share is larger again. Comité figures quoted in the trade have put it at close to four-fifths of the region's turnover.
Put the two halves side by side and the shape of the region appears. Most of the land is farmed by growers, while most of the wine is made and sold by houses.
What joins them is the sale of grapes. Most of the grapes that growers harvest each autumn are sold to the houses rather than made into wine by the growers themselves.
A house can therefore draw on many villages at once, which is what makes assemblage, the art of blending wines from different places, grapes and years, possible on a large scale.
A grower usually works a far smaller patchwork of plots, often within one village and its neighbours, so a grower's own wine tends to speak of a smaller place.
On the label, a small code tells you which kind of producer made the wine. NM marks a négociant-manipulant, a house, and RM a récoltant-manipulant, a grower who makes their own.
There are other codes too, such as CM for a cooperative, and we will come to them later. For now, NM and RM are a good place to begin.
Neither side could have made champagne what it is alone. The houses needed the growers' grapes, the growers needed someone to buy them, and that has been true for close to three centuries.
How the balance between them moved, who held the money and who farmed the vines, is the story this thread follows, beginning with the rise of the houses.
episodes.setup: The houses came first, and they were born in a world of cloth merchants, royal decrees and baskets of bottles. Next, we go back to the eighteenth century to meet them.

episodes.title: How the Great Houses Rose
episodes.hook: Many of the names on the grandest champagne labels are old, and a good number of them began not with a vineyard but with a merchant's ledger. To see why, it helps to look at what selling sparkling wine actually demanded.
episodes.callback: We saw that growers farm most of the vines, while houses ship most of the bottles.
cards: For a long time the wines of Champagne travelled in wooden barrels, as the rules required. That kept any trade in wine already in bottle small and close to home.
In 1728 a royal decree changed that, permitting the region's wine to be sent in baskets of bottles, which opened the way to customers far beyond Champagne.
The next year, on 1 September 1729, Nicolas Ruinart, of a Reims family in the cloth trade, recorded the founding of his wine business in his account book.
His first wines went out as gifts to the family's cloth customers, and within a few years wine had become the business itself, with the cloth left behind.
Ruinart is usually called the oldest established champagne house, meaning the oldest business founded to trade in champagne, and that is how the house tells its own story.
Gosset, in Aÿ, makes a rival claim. It dates its roots to 1584, to a grower making still wine, mostly red, long before Champagne was known for its bubbles.
Both claims can stand together, because they measure different things. One counts the oldest family making wine, the other the oldest business built around the sparkling wine.
More houses followed in the eighteenth century. Claude Moët, a wine trader, founded his house in Épernay in 1743, and Philippe Clicquot founded his in Reims in 1772.
In 1785 Florens-Louis Heidsieck, a cloth merchant from Westphalia, founded his house in Reims. He is described as the first of several German founders to settle in Champagne.
Others came in the following decades. The Mumm brothers, sons of a German wine merchant, began in Reims in 1827, and Bollinger was founded in Aÿ in 1829 with a German-born partner.
Deutz followed in Aÿ in 1838, founded by two Germans, and in 1843 a Mainz-born former bookkeeper at another champagne house founded Krug in Reims.
Look at those founders and a pattern appears. Many were traders, bookkeepers and merchants, people who already understood credit, customers and the long roads of export.
Not all of them came from commerce, since some of the German newcomers were the sons of winegrowers at home. What they shared was that they set up here as merchants.
It helps to think about what sparkling wine asks of a business. The wine has to rest in the bottle for many months before it can be sold, and money is tied up all that time.
Today the rules require at least fifteen months before a non-vintage champagne is released, and three years for a vintage. Every one of those months is money resting in a cellar.
The second fermentation that makes the bubbles, the prise de mousse, happens inside the bottle, and in the early days bottles could burst in the cellar, a costly risk to carry.
Then there were the cellars themselves, cool and deep enough to hold many thousands of bottles for years, which took capital to dig, to buy or to rent.
And there were the buyers, in Paris, London and well beyond, who had to be found, visited, trusted and paid. A merchant's network could be worth as much as the wine.
A grower with a few plots, and a harvest to bring in every autumn, could rarely carry all of that at once. Selling the grapes, and being paid that season, made good sense.
Seen this way, the division of labour grew out of the work itself. The houses gathered capital, cellars and customers, while the growers did what no house could do alone, which was farm the vines.
episodes.setup: For more than a century most growers stayed on their side of that line. Next, we look at why they waited so long to make wine of their own, and what finally changed.

episodes.title: The Growers' Long Wait
episodes.hook: For generations, a Champagne grower's year ended with the harvest sold to a house. Making and selling your own champagne was possible, but rare, and the reasons had as much to do with money and risk as with skill.
episodes.callback: We met the merchants who built the first houses, with their cellars, their credit and their customers abroad.
cards: A grower who sells grapes is paid for that year's work without a long wait. A grower who makes champagne waits many months, often years, before the first bottle can be sold.
That difference shaped everything. Making champagne meant pressing, fermenting, bottling and ageing, then finding buyers, all paid for long before any money came back.
Some growers did take that step early. The region's own accounts mention growers making their own champagne from the early nineteenth century, though it remained very unusual.
Those early pioneers were found mostly around Épernay, and one account records a grower in the village of Boursault making champagne as early as 1876.
A grower who does this is called a récoltant-manipulant. Récoltant means harvester, and manipulant means one who handles the wine, in other words the person who actually makes it.
For most growers, though, the houses were the market, and the price they paid for grapes decided whether a family prospered or struggled that year.
That dependence left growers exposed. In bad years, when frost, disease or poor sales struck, they had little to fall back on but the vines themselves.
The early twentieth century brought hard years and open anger. In 1911 growers rioted in the Marne, angered in part by grapes from outside the region being used for champagne.
Those riots are often described as one of the pressures that pushed the region toward firm rules on where champagne may come from, which steadied the growers' place in the trade.
Then came the Great Depression. By the houses' own account, grape prices fell tenfold, to less than one franc a kilo, and some vineyards were at risk of being abandoned.
Growers and houses each had their own unions, but agreeing a fair price was one thing and making it stick was another, because neither union had any power to enforce it.
After the crash of 1929, the Prefect, the state's representative in the département, had to step in and fix a minimum price for grapes.
In 1935 a joint body, the Commission de Châlons, was created to set minimum prices with both sides at the table, and grapes bought below that price could not be used for champagne.
In 1941 the region created the Comité Interprofessionnel du Vin de Champagne, the CIVC, a joint body for growers and houses that continues today as the Comité Champagne.
Hard times also pushed some growers to stop depending on a buyer at all. One history says grower bottling quickened in the 1930s, when selling grapes to the houses grew difficult.
Even so, until the middle of the twentieth century almost all growers still sold their grapes to the houses, and their own bottles remained a small part of the trade.
The larger change came after the Second World War. From the 1950s, more growers began to make champagne and sell it under their own names.
Not every grower could do that alone, with a press, a cellar and a stock of bottles of their own. Many found another way, by joining together with their neighbours.
That other way, the cooperative, gave a family the tools of a house without asking it to build one, and it began to change the balance of the region.
episodes.setup: Next, we visit the cooperatives: why growers joined together, how one village's early attempt was received by the houses, and what the letters CM on a label mean.

episodes.title: The Cooperatives
episodes.hook: A cooperative lets a village's growers share a press house, a cellar and sometimes a brand. In Champagne, cooperatives began partly as a way to bargain with the houses, and they grew into one of the region's three kinds of producer.
episodes.callback: We followed the growers through riots, the Depression and the first minimum prices for grapes.
cards: A cooperative, in French a coopérative, is a business held jointly by its members, who share its equipment and its costs and divide what it earns.
In Champagne the members are growers. They bring their grapes to a shared press house and cellar, which few of them could easily afford alone.
The region's cooperatives are often traced to the early twentieth century, the same unsettled years of growers' protest that surrounded the riots of 1911.
One of the oldest still working is in the grand cru village of Mailly-Champagne, on the Montagne de Reims, founded in 1929, the year the Great Depression began.
By the cooperative's own account, about two dozen growers of the village joined forces to win a better price for the wine they sold to the houses.
The houses, it says, would have none of it, keen to keep down the price of the grapes they bought, and for its first two years the new venture did no business at all.
So the growers decided to make and sell champagne themselves, with rented equipment and recycled bottles, and in time they sold all 3,600 bottles to a single buyer.
It is the cooperative's own story, told with pride, but it captures something real. A cooperative let growers become makers of wine, and not only sellers of grapes.
Many cooperatives began by pressing and storing their members' harvests, which gave growers more time, and a stronger hand, when they came to bargain with the houses.
Others went further and built brands of their own. More followed through the century, such as one in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger in 1937 and Union Champagne in Avize in 1966.
Then cooperatives began to join other cooperatives. The Centre Vinicole de la Champagne began as a union of cooperatives, with sources placing its start in 1971 or 1972.
It later took on the Nicolas Feuillatte brand, which was created in 1976 and bought by the Centre Vinicole in 1986, and which has become a familiar name in France and abroad.
The label shows when a cooperative made the wine. CM stands for coopérative de manipulation, a cooperative that makes champagne from its members' grapes and sells it under its own brands.
A related code, RC, stands for récoltant-coopérateur. The grower's wine is made at the cooperative, and the grower then sells it under the family's own name.
That makes an RC bottle easy to mistake for one made entirely at the grower's own cellar, which would be marked RM. The two codes are there to tell them apart.
Another, MA, stands for marque d'acheteur, a buyer's own brand, such as a shop's own label, where the wine was made by someone else and the code says so.
In the Comité's 2025 figures there were 120 cooperatives, and that year, by one trade analysis, they shipped about 23 million bottles under their own names, a little under one in ten.
Their quieter role matters as much as their brands. By pressing and keeping grapes for their members, cooperatives gave many growers choices they had not had before.
A grower in a cooperative could sell to a house, or take finished bottles home to sell under the family name. Having a choice is itself a kind of strength.
And it helped set the stage for the growers who wanted to do everything themselves, from the vine to the bottle, and whose wines would one day travel far beyond their villages.
episodes.setup: Next, the growers who bottle their own: how récoltant-manipulant champagne found admirers abroad, and why its share of the market tells a more surprising story.

episodes.title: The Grower Movement
episodes.hook: Over the past few decades, grower champagne has become a phrase that wine lovers say with real affection. Its reputation has grown remarkably, and yet the numbers behind it describe something quieter, and more interesting, than a takeover.
episodes.callback: We saw cooperatives give growers presses, cellars and a choice about where their grapes went.
cards: Grower champagne is the everyday name for wine made by a récoltant-manipulant, a grower who farms the vines, makes the wine and sells it under their own name, marked RM on the label.
A grower's vineyards are usually few and often close to one village, so the wine tends to carry the character of that place and of that family's way of working.
That is the deep difference from a house, whose skill lies in assemblage, blending many villages and years to keep one recognisable style from one year to the next.
Neither approach is better by nature. A blend can be magnificent and a single-village wine can be ordinary. They simply answer different questions about what champagne is for.
In the 1990s, a few importers in the United States began to seek out these wines and champion them, and the idea of grower champagne began to take shape abroad.
Admirers were drawn to wines that tasted of one village, sometimes of one named plot, a lieu-dit, and often to growers working with organic or low-intervention methods.
Some growers bottled a single plot on its own, a choice that the blending tradition of the great houses had never been designed to make.
An importer writing in 2026 described steady growth in the United States since the mid-2010s, with grower bottles now turning up even in ordinary wine shops there.
So it would be natural to imagine growers taking a larger and larger share of champagne's sales. The numbers tell a different, gentler story.
Growers who sell their own champagne once shipped roughly a quarter of the region's bottles. Trade analyses date that high point differently, somewhere between about 2000 and 2008.
In 2025, by one trade analysis of the Comité's figures, growers shipped about 51 million bottles, a little under a fifth of the total.
Most of that wine never leaves France. In 2019 growers sold about 85 per cent of their own bottles at home and exported around 8 million.
That same year, of about 15,800 growers, close to 4,000 sold champagne of their own, and only around 1,300 sent any of it outside France.
So roughly three growers in every four sold no champagne under their own name that year, and placed their grapes or wine elsewhere, with houses or cooperatives.
The grower movement is real, then, but small in bottles. Its reputation abroad rests on a few thousand estates, and on the smaller number of them that export.
Why has the growers' share of bottles fallen while their reputation grew? Sources do not offer one tidy answer, and it is wise to be careful with any single explanation.
What can be said is that making, storing and selling champagne still asks for money, time and risk, while selling grapes to a house still brings payment for the harvest.
Seen that way, the grower movement is less a revolution than a widening of choice, for growers deciding what to do with their grapes and for drinkers deciding what to pour.
And it gives you something lovely to look for. Two letters on a back label, RM, tell you that one family carried the wine all the way from vine to bottle.
episodes.setup: While growers were learning to sell the character of a village, the houses had been building something quite different at the very top. Next, the invention of the prestige cuvée.

episodes.title: Prestige Cuvées
episodes.hook: At the top of many houses' ranges sits a bottle made in small quantities and sold for a much higher price. That luxury tier has a history, and its two most famous origin stories are worth telling carefully.
episodes.callback: We saw grower champagne win admirers abroad while its share of bottles stayed small.
cards: A cuvée de prestige, or prestige cuvée, is a house's finest wine, often from a single year and from its most prized grapes, presented as something apart from the rest of its range.
The two stories told most often about how this tier began belong to Louis Roederer's Cristal and to Moët & Chandon's Dom Pérignon.
Roederer says that Cristal was created in 1876 for Tsar Alexander II of Russia, who asked the house to reserve its best cuvée for him every year.
It came in a clear, flat-bottomed bottle of lead crystal, which gave the wine its name, and which let the Tsar see the colour and the bubbles of what he was served.
A popular version adds that the flat base and clear glass were meant to stop anyone hiding a bomb beneath the bottle. Given the dangers a tsar faced, it is easy to see why the story stuck.
It is, however, a story without firm evidence behind it. Even the online encyclopaedia that repeats it marks the claim as needing a source, so it is best enjoyed as legend.
Cristal was a wine for the Russian court, and Roederer did not present it to the public as a luxury champagne in the way we would understand that today.
The house kept making it after the Russian monarchy fell in 1917, and most sources place its first public sale in 1945, though some tie that date to a vintage instead.
Dom Pérignon's story begins with a name. Dom Pierre Pérignon was a Benedictine monk at the abbey of Hautvillers, near Épernay, much loved in Champagne's history and its legends.
The brand name was first registered by the house of Mercier, and it passed to Moët & Chandon in 1927, on the occasion of a marriage between the two families.
The first wine sold under the name was the 1921 vintage. It went on sale in 1936 and, by several accounts, crossed to New York aboard the liner Normandie.
A year earlier, in 1935, Moët's London importer had received a special bottling of an older vintage to mark its centenary, which some count as a forerunner.
That is why you may meet both 1935 and 1936 in the story. The 1921 vintage released in 1936 is what most sources treat as Dom Pérignon's commercial debut.
Both wines can be called the first, depending on what you count. Cristal was made first, for one customer. Dom Pérignon was the first to be launched and sold as a prestige cuvée.
Other houses followed in the decades after the war. Taittinger's Comtes de Champagne, for example, has a first vintage of 1952, according to one specialist source.
More launches came from the 1960s onward, though sources give different years for several of them, so we have not tried to put them in order here.
Why did the idea succeed? A prestige cuvée lets a house show the very best its cellars can do, and the price gives that best a shape that people recognise.
It also raises the stakes between houses and growers, because the finest grapes from the most admired villages are worth even more when they end up in the costliest bottles.
For you, a prestige cuvée is a house at its most ambitious. It is worth trying once, with a little curiosity, beside that same house's ordinary non-vintage wine.
episodes.setup: The houses that made those bottles once called the best known among them the grandes marques. Next, what that title meant, why it faded, and how houses and growers do business today.

episodes.title: The Grandes Marques and Today's Market
episodes.hook: For much of the twentieth century, the best-known houses were spoken of as the grandes marques, the great brands. The title has faded, but the relationship beneath it, between the houses and the growers who supply them, matters as much as ever.
episodes.callback: We traced the prestige cuvée from a tsar's table in 1876 to a liner bound for New York in 1936.
cards: The houses first organised themselves in 1882, when thirty-five of them formed the Syndicat du Commerce des Vins de Champagne, above all to protect the name Champagne from imitators.
Among the early results was a court ruling of 1887 that the name Champagne referred to wines of a particular place and method, a judgement confirmed in 1889.
Over time, the best-known houses came to be called the grandes marques, the great brands, a phrase that sounded to many buyers like a promise of quality.
Before 1994, the houses' trade body was a federation of two groups, one for the grandes marques and one for the other merchant houses, the négociants.
From 1994 the houses joined the Union des Maisons de Champagne directly, and the separate association of grandes marques was disbanded in 1997.
One account says it ended after its members could not agree on what quality standards membership should demand. We found only that one account, so please hold it lightly.
The phrase still turns up today, in conversation and in the houses' own literature, but it no longer has a settled definition.
Behind every great brand, though, lay the practical question that runs through this whole thread, which is how a house can be sure of enough good grapes each year.
In 1959 the two sides agreed a contrat interprofessionnel, a contract for the whole trade, under which growers sold grapes to the houses at a price linked to the price of a bottle.
The first edition set the grape price at 28 per cent of the bottle's price, and later editions moved between 32 and 36 per cent, with the CIVC sharing out the contracted crop.

The contract ran through five successive editions over three decades. When work on a sixth began in 1990 the idea was dropped, and the trade returned to contracts between individual growers and houses.
The houses' own history notes a drawback of the old system, which is that a price set for everyone gave growers little reason to raise the quality of their grapes.
Today there is no shared grape price agreed for everyone, since fixing prices jointly would sit badly with European competition rules. Growers and houses negotiate their own contracts.
Contracts lasting several years have long been common, an arrangement that gives a grower a dependable buyer and gives a house a dependable supply.
Grapes are a large part of what a bottle costs. The houses' trade union puts them at about 36 per cent of the average bottle's price, a share it describes as steady over a decade.
The two sides still meet within the Comité Champagne, where each year they agree the rendement, the weight of grapes per hectare that may be harvested and sold as champagne.
For 2025 that figure was set at 9,000 kilograms per hectare, about a thousand below the year before, to slow the build-up of stocks while sales were slower.
Among the houses, many famous names now sit within larger groups. The leading group, LVMH, includes Moët & Chandon, Veuve Clicquot, Krug, Mercier and Dom Pérignon, among others.
Brands also change hands between groups. In 2025, Vranken-Pommery agreed to sell its Heidsieck & Co Monopole business to Lanson-BCC, another of the region's groups.
Groups change, brands move and contracts are renegotiated, but the arrangement underneath has held. Houses need the growers' grapes, and growers need buyers for them.
That is why the code on the back label, NM or RM or CM, is worth a glance. It tells you which side of this long partnership made the wine in your glass.
episodes.setup: That brings the story up to the present. To close, we gather what has held up, what has changed, which popular versions deserve a gentle correction, and what we left out.

episodes.title: Scorecard
episodes.hook: Every thread here ends with an honest account. This is where we gather what has held up, what has been overtaken by events, and what we chose to leave out, with our reasons, so that you can trust the rest.
episodes.callback: We ended with the rendement agreed each year, and with famous brands moving between groups.
cards: First, what has held. Growers still farm close to nine-tenths of Champagne's vineyard area, and houses still ship around seven bottles in every ten.
Most growers still sell some or all of their grapes rather than bottling everything themselves, much as they did when the first houses were founded.
Ruinart's founding on 1 September 1729, and the founding dates of the other houses we named, are consistent across the sources we checked.
Cristal's creation in 1876 for Tsar Alexander II, as Roederer tells it, and the release of Dom Pérignon's 1921 vintage in 1936 are both well supported.
Next, what has been overtaken. The single grape price that once bound the whole region together ended with the old contract system, after 1990.
The grandes marques association no longer exists, although the phrase lives on, and the houses now belong directly to the Union des Maisons de Champagne.
The growers' share of bottles has fallen from roughly a quarter to a little under a fifth, even as their reputation abroad has grown.
Some popular versions deserve a gentle correction. Ruinart is the oldest house founded to trade in champagne, while Gosset's older roots lie in still wine. Both claims can stand.
The tale of a bomb-proof bottle for the Tsar is a lovely one, but it has no firm evidence behind it, and we have told it here as legend.
Cristal was made first, but it was not sold to the public until much later. Dom Pérignon was the first prestige cuvée to be launched as one, in 1936.
Grower champagne has not overtaken the houses. It remains a modest share of bottles, most of it drunk in France, and only a minority of growers export at all.
Finally, what we left out, and why. Counts of growers, houses and cooperatives differ between years and sources, so we gave the Comité's 2025 figures and named the year.
We gave only an approximate share of sales by value for the houses, because the most precise figure we found was older and its year was unclear.
We gave no single count of récoltants-manipulants today. Estimates we found ran from about two thousand to about five thousand, and we could not confirm an official figure.
We did not say how many bottles of the first Dom Pérignon were sold, because accounts differ, nor exactly how its early bottlings related to Moët's own vintage wine.
We left out the launch years of several later prestige cuvées, such as Perrier-Jouët's Belle Époque, because the sources we found disagree by several years.
We left out the price paid when Heidsieck & Co Monopole changed hands, because reports gave very different figures, and we gave no grape prices per kilo, for want of current official ones.
And we did not say why the growers' share of bottles has fallen. Several explanations are offered, and none was well enough sourced to put on a card.
Thank you for reading this far. We hope that next time you turn a bottle around to find those small letters, you will see the two families of people behind it.
